nameStory: The Red Tree Brain Fungus gets its distinctive name from its wrinkled, coral-red surface that looks remarkably like brain tissue spread across tree bark. When fresh, the convoluted folds and creases create an unmistakable resemblance to neural matter, making this one of the most memorably named fungi you'll encounter.
description: Red Tree Brain Fungus is a crust fungus that forms thin, leathery patches directly on the bark of dead hardwood trees. Rather than having a traditional mushroom shape with cap and stem, it grows as a flat, encrusting layer that can spread several inches across the bark surface. The fungus starts small but can expand to cover areas up to 6 inches wide, creating distinctive brain-like wrinkles and folds as it matures.

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: The defining feature is the wrinkled, brain-like surface with deep folds and ridges that feel leathery but slightly soft when fresh, becoming harder and more brittle when dry

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Bright coral-red to orange-red when fresh and moist, fading to dull reddish-brown or tan as it dries out

idTips.label: Growth Pattern
idTips.description: Forms flat, crust-like patches that spread directly across bark surfaces without any stem or cap structure

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Found exclusively on dead hardwood bark, particularly oak, maple, and birch, never on living trees or other surfaces

idTips.label: Thickness
idTips.description: Creates a coating roughly 1-3mm thick that you can feel protruding slightly from the bark surface

habitat: Red Tree Brain Fungus appears on dead branches and fallen logs of hardwood trees throughout New England's deciduous and mixed forests. It particularly favors oak, maple, and birch bark in areas with consistent moisture, often found in shaded woodland areas where humidity remains higher. You'll spot it from sea level up through mid-elevation forests, typically on branches that are 1-4 inches in diameter.

seasonality.spring: Fresh growth begins as temperatures warm and spring rains provide moisture, appearing as small bright red patches that start developing their characteristic wrinkled texture.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when specimens are most vibrant and extensive, with the brain-like folds fully developed and coral-red coloration at its brightest.
seasonality.fall: Continues growing through early fall but begins to fade and dry out, becoming more brownish and leathery as temperatures drop and humidity decreases.
seasonality.winter: Persists as dried, brittle remnants on bark that are tan to brown in color, though they're much less noticeable and harder to identify in this dormant state.

funFact: This fungus literally dissolves wood from the inside out using powerful enzymes, but it's so precise that it can completely consume the cellulose and lignin while leaving the bark structure intact—like eating the filling out of a sandwich while keeping the bread perfectly whole.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other red crust fungi, but Red Tree Brain Fungus is the only one with pronounced brain-like wrinkles—other red crusts are either smooth, bumpy, or have tiny pores but lack the deep folded texture. Remember: if it looks like red brain coral on bark, you've found your match.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'tree brain' fungus, it only grows on dead wood and is actually helping the forest by breaking down dead material—it's not harming living trees. The scientific name Peniophora comes from Greek words meaning 'thread-bearing,' referring to microscopic features invisible to the naked eye.
compareHints: Red Tree Brain Fungus stands out from its Peniophora relatives by having the most pronounced wrinkled surface texture—Giraffe Spots has a spotted appearance without deep folds, while Rosy Crust is much smoother and pinker. The deep brain-like convolutions are unique to this species in the genus, making it the easiest Peniophora to identify in the field.
